items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Big Eye Louis Nelson, I played with him. He was crazy about me.

ctx.x: Then you started playing with other bands. Did you ever play with a lot of older musicians here, like your uncles and people like that.

My uncles, they were young like me. They’re just about 8, 10 years older than me. I played with some ancient musicians, like Old Man George Glenny. Big Eye Louis Nelson, I played with him. He was crazy about me. He liked me, because I was dressed up all the time. He said, “You’re on the right track with your big papas. You’re on the right track, kid. You keep neat. People call in town.” I said, “Thank you Mr. Louis.” Big Eye, I played with him. Played with so many other musicians that phased out. Can’t think of…

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: Big-Eye Louis [Nelson] was a great clarinet player, who was somewhat of a rival of Tio. Big-Eye Louis and Picou, they were masters of that style of playing, that improvisation...

ctx.x: Well, he had been on the Orpheum circuit for about ten years, from about 1909, the year I was born, until, what, 1918 or 1919, when the Dixieland Band recorded... Them people had been on the Orpheum circuit, him and Big-Eye Louis, a band from New Orleans...

items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1959-06-30
items.q: I worked with him, I know him at Twy, and Walter DeCoult, four of us at the Bungalow.

ctx.x: Willie Humphrey, the one that's working with Paul now. Earl Humphrey's brother. He impressed me, but he lived uptown and never had a chance much to him. And he's the one that impressed me, I thought he was a master. There were others, like Big Al Lloyd, who was always in the same track in the summer of retirement. He played if he got a chance.
